title: Docker Architecture
subtitle: What happens between the CLI and a running process
description: A precise tour of the Docker client, daemon, containerd, runc, namespaces and cgroups. This is the knowledge that turns confusing errors into obvious ones.
outcomes: Trace a docker run request through every component
Explain the role of containerd and runc
Describe how namespaces and cgroups isolate and limit a process

modules.title: Components
modules.summary: The moving parts of a Docker installation.

lessons.title: Client, daemon and API
lessons.summary: The CLI is a thin HTTP client. Almost everything interesting happens in the daemon.
objectives: Explain the Docker API and socket
Know what happens when the daemon is unreachable

sections.title: A REST API with a CLI on top
sections.body:
The `docker` command parses your arguments and sends an HTTP request to the Docker daemon over a Unix socket (`/var/run/docker.sock` by default) or a TCP endpoint. The daemon does the work: pulling, building, creating, starting, and streaming logs back.

This is why remote Docker works, why tools such as Portainer and CI runners can control Docker without the CLI, and why protecting the socket is equivalent to protecting root.

sections.caption: Client → daemon → containerd → runc → process. The registry is contacted by the daemon, not by your CLI.

head: Component
Responsibility
rows: Argument parsing, API calls, output formatting
Image store, networks, volumes, API, orchestration of containers
Creates namespaces/cgroups and execs the container process

sections.title: Remote engines are just contexts
sections.body: `docker context create` stores an endpoint; `docker context use` switches the CLI to it. The CLI itself does not change.

exercises.title: Inspect the endpoint
exercises.prompt: Print the Docker host and context currently in use.
exercises.expected: DOCKER_HOST may be empty (default socket) and `docker context show` prints the context name.

exercises.title: Explain the split
exercises.prompt: Why can a CI runner control a remote Docker engine without installing the daemon locally?
exercises.expected: It only needs the client and access to the API endpoint.

questions.question: Who pulls an image during docker run?
questions.explain: The daemon performs image operations and reports progress to the client.

questions.question: The default Docker endpoint is…
questions.explain: Linux uses /var/run/docker.sock by default. Windows uses a named pipe.

questions.question: Why is docker.sock access dangerous?
options: It is writable by all users by default
It grants control equivalent to root
questions.explain: The daemon can start privileged containers and mount host paths.

lessons.title: dockerd, containerd and runc
lessons.summary: The chain of custody for a container process, and why it matters when something fails to start.
objectives: Name the responsibility of each layer
Read a container start failure with the right mental model

sections.title: Three layers, one process
sections.body:
`dockerd` is the API server and the orchestrator of Docker objects. It delegates container execution to **containerd**, a general-purpose container runtime. containerd prepares the image snapshot and root filesystem, then invokes **runc**, an OCI runtime that creates namespaces and cgroups and execs the process.

A **shim** (containerd-shim-runc-v2) sits between containerd and the container process. It keeps the container alive if containerd restarts and collects the exit status. That is why `docker ps` can still work while the daemon is being upgraded.

sections.caption: dockerd → containerd → shim → runc → container process.

sections.code:
# See the runtime chain
ps -eo pid,ppid,comm,args | grep -E 'dockerd|containerd|shim|runc' | grep -v grep

docker info --format '{{.Driver}} {{.CgroupDriver}} {{.KernelVersion}}'
sections.note: Runc only exists while a container is being created. After exec, the shim supervises the process.

sections.title: Do not restart dockerd to fix one container
sections.body: Restarting the daemon can disrupt networking and running containers. Diagnose with `docker inspect`, `docker logs`, and `journalctl -u docker` first.

exercises.title: Find the chain
exercises.prompt: Run a sleep container and identify its shim and runtime processes.
exercises.expected: A containerd-shim-runc-v2 process appears between containerd and the sleep process.

exercises.title: Read the driver
exercises.prompt: Print the storage driver, cgroup driver and kernel version.

questions.question: Which component creates namespaces and cgroups?
questions.explain: runc implements the OCI runtime steps that isolate the process.

questions.question: What is the shim responsible for?
options: Supervising a container process and reporting exit status
questions.explain: The shim outlives containerd restarts and owns the process lifecycle.

questions.question: Where do you look for daemon-level errors?
questions.explain: The daemon logs to the system journal on systemd hosts.

lessons.title: Namespaces and cgroups
lessons.summary: The two Linux features that make containers possible: isolation and limits.
objectives: List the namespaces a container gets
Recognise the limits of container isolation

sections.title: Namespaces isolate what a process can see
sections.body:
A namespace wraps a global system resource so processes inside it see their own private view. Docker uses PID, mount, network, IPC, UTS, user and cgroup namespaces. The PID namespace is why the container main process appears as PID 1 inside the container while having a different host PID.

Namespaces do not limit resources — they only change visibility. Two containers can each see "their" network stack while still competing for host CPU.

sections.title: Cgroups limit what a process can use
sections.body: Control groups account for and constrain CPU, memory, block I/O and process counts. `--cpus`, `--memory`, `--pids-limit` and `--blkio-weight` map to cgroup controls. When a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel OOM killer terminates processes inside it; the container exits with code 137.

sections.title: Containers are not a security boundary by default
sections.body: A kernel exploit or a privileged container can escape to the host. Harden with non-root users, dropped capabilities, seccomp, read-only filesystems and user namespaces.

exercises.title: See the namespaces
exercises.prompt: Run a container and list its namespaces from the host.
exercises.command:
docker run -d --name ns-demo alpine sleep 300
docker inspect ns-demo --format '{{.State.Pid}}'
exercises.expected: lsns or /proc/<pid>/ns shows pid, net, mnt, ipc, uts, user namespaces.

exercises.title: Trigger the limit
exercises.prompt: Run a container with --memory 32m that allocates more and observe exit code 137.
exercises.expected: The process is OOM-killed and docker inspect reports OOMKilled=true.

questions.question: Which feature limits a container to 512 MB of memory?
Why does the container process see PID 1?
options: It really is the host init
questions.explain: Inside the PID namespace the first process is 1.

questions.question: Exit code 137 usually means…
options: The process was killed, often by the OOM killer
questions.explain: 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), commonly caused by exceeding a memory limit.
